title: Chemical-Disorder-Induced Non-metallic Transport in Thermodynamically Metallic Mo4TGa16Ge (T = Co, Rh or Ir)
authors: Chaoguo Wang, Jiaqi Tian, Xin Gui
abstract: Flat-band electronic states can be highly sensitive to chemical perturbations, offering opportunities to access a broader range of electronic behaviors beyond that of parent materials. Here, we report the discovery of a new series of compounds, Mo4TGa16Ge (T = Co, Rh, or Ir), derived from the strongly correlated flat-band superconductor, Mo4PtGa17, via nominally preserving the total valence electron counts. All three materials crystallize in a noncentrosymmetric cubic space group, F-43m, with Ge selectively occupying one of the Ga sites in the parent compound. Although the total electron count remains the same, Mo4TGa16Ge exhibits significantly distinct properties from Mo4PtGa17. Theoretical calculations predict metallic electronic structures with narrow, dominant Mo-d states at the Fermi energy, while low-temperature heat capacity results demonstrate finite Sommerfeld coefficients. However, electrical transport measurements show predominantly non-metallic behaviors with small observed activation energies, excluding the possibilities of conventional semiconducting behaviors. Combining chemical bonding analysis, electronic structure and compositional determination from X-ray crystallography and spectroscopy, we propose that the coexistence of the non-metallic transport features and the thermodynamically metallic behaviors can be attributed to the high sensitivity of the narrow-band materials to chemical disorders. Thus, the discovery and investigation of Mo4TGa16Ge provide a chemically tunable platform for studying disorder-controlled transport in flat-band intermetallics.
summary: This work explores the $	ext{Mo}_4	ext{TGa}_{16}	ext{Ge}$ compounds, which possess flat-band electronic characteristics. The researchers found a conflict between theoretical predictions of metallic behavior and experimental measurements showing non-metallic transport. They resolve this by proposing that chemical disorder, induced by the substitution of elements, is responsible for suppressing the metallic transport properties in these sensitive intermetallics.
main_problem: The paper investigates the origin of non-metallic electrical transport features that coexist with thermodynamically metallic electronic signatures in a new series of compounds.
main_result: The discrepancy is attributed to the high sensitivity of narrow-band materials to chemical disorders, suggesting a chemically tunable platform for studying disorder-controlled transport.
method: The study combines theoretical calculations (DFT, COHP/ICOHP) with extensive experimental measurements, including transport ($ho(T)$), heat capacity ($C_p(T)$), and X-ray crystallography.
model_or_system: The physical system is the $	ext{Mo}_4	ext{TGa}_{16}	ext{Ge}$ series ($	ext{T} = 	ext{Co}, 	ext{Rh}, 	ext{or Ir}$), derived from the flat-band superconductor $	ext{Mo}_4	ext{PtGa}_{17}$. These compounds are structurally related and exhibit flat-band electronic states.
key_observables: Electrical resistivity ($ho(T)$), Sommerfeld coefficient ($\gamma$) from $C_p(T)$, electronic band structure, and chemical bonding analysis via COHP/ICOHP.
important_parameters: Low temperatures, Fermi energy ($E_F$), and the chemical identity of the transition metal T ($	ext{Co}, 	ext{Rh}, 	ext{Ir}$).
main_assumptions: The non-metallic transport features are not intrinsic semiconducting gaps but are instead induced by chemical disorder effects on the narrow-band electronic structure.
figures_summary: Figures detail the crystal structure, XRD patterns, magnetic susceptibility, temperature-dependent heat capacity, electronic band structures, and resistivity measurements for the studied compounds.
paper_structure: The paper follows a structure of structural characterization (XRD, composition) $\rightarrow$ electronic structure analysis (DFT, bonding) $\rightarrow$ thermodynamic measurements ($C_p(T)$) $\rightarrow$ transport measurements ($ho(T)$), culminating in a unified explanation linking disorder to the observed transport paradox.
why_interesting: The study directly addresses the interplay between electronic structure theory (flat bands, correlation) and real-world material imperfections (chemical disorder), which is a key area in strongly correlated electron physics.
